title: compassion
hookLine: compassion — metta when it meets pain
last: METTA — MAY YOU BE AT EASE.

cards: A friend calls, and you can hear right away that something's wrong. The first instinct might be to fix it. Give advice.
Find the silver lining. Change the subject to something lighter. Or the instinct might be to back away a little, because their pain is heavy and there's your own day to get through.
Both are normal. Both are ways of leaving. There's a third thing a person can do, and it's much harder than fixing or leaving.
You can stay. Today, what metta becomes when it meets pain.

teach.b: It's the second of four qualities Buddhists call the brahmaviharas, the divine abodes, places a heart can live. Metta, friendliness. Karuna, compassion.
Mudita, gladness at others' good fortune. And upekkha, a steady calm, which you'll meet in a few days. Metta wishes someone well.

Karuna is what happens when that wish runs into someone's pain. An old commentary, Buddhaghosa's, explains the word this way: compassion is what makes a good heart tremble when others suffer. It doesn't turn away.
It quivers, and stays. The same commentary warns about two traps. Compassion's far enemy is cruelty, the plain opposite.
Its near enemy is sneakier: a worldly grief that looks like compassion but is really sorrow for oneself. Some modern teachers put the near enemy as pity.
Pity looks down: oh, you poor thing, glad that isn't me. Compassion stands beside. There's a story in the monastic rules about this.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA WASHES THE SICK MONK.
teach.b: The Buddha and his attendant Ananda find a monk lying sick in his own filth, and nobody is caring for him. The Buddha washes him himself, with Ananda's help.
Then he gathers the monks and says, in effect: you have no mother or father here to care for you.
If you don't care for each other, who will? Whoever would care for me should care for the sick.

In Mahayana Buddhism, compassion is embodied by Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world, known as Guanyin in China and Chenrezig in Tibet. But it can start very simply. Someone is hurting.

how: Buddhists cultivate karuna in meditation, extending the wish that beings be free from suffering, and in action: caring for the sick, the poor and animals; in Mahayana traditions people recite the names or mantra of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a grief that only looks like it
the bodhisattva who hears the world's cries

s: compassion and pity are the same thing
pity looks down. compassion stands beside. some teachers call pity its near enemy.
the Buddha himself washed a sick monk nobody was caring for
and told the monks: whoever would care for me should care for the sick.
karuna is the second of the four divine abodes

games.q: the Buddha finds a monk lying sick and alone, and nobody is looking after him. what does he do?
o: sends someone to find a doctor.
washes and cares for him himself.
asks the monk what he did to deserve it.
games.why: he washes the monk himself, with Ananda's help, then tells the monks: whoever would care for me should care for the sick.

practice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Bring to mind someone who's hurting right now. Someone you know, or someone you saw on the news.
Let yourself feel a little of it. Not all of it, just enough that your heart moves. Notice any urge to fix it, or to pull away.
Don't act on either. Just stay with them in your mind, breathing. If you like, let a wish go toward them: may you be free from this pain.

wordCard.voice: Karuna. Compassion: metta when it meets pain, the heart that trembles and stays beside, not above. Sixteenth word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: compassion. The second of the four brahmavihāras.

carryVoice: Your line: stay. Not fixing, not leaving: staying is its own kind of help. See you tomorrow.
